**found and fixed, and it was never a mobile bug.** `AGameModeBase::RestartPlayerAtPlayerStart` builds the spawn rotation from **yaw alone** and discards pitch and roll — stock engine behaviour, sensible on a flat map and meaningless on a sphere. The saved PlayerStart is correct (**+0.0°** against its own local up); the pawn was handed `(0, 33.41, 0)`, whose forward dots to −0.708 with local up → **−45.1°**. Reproduced on PC in any standalone `-game` session and invisible in PIE, which is why it looked like a phone fault. The character now takes its facing from the PlayerStart, which still has all three angles, and projects it onto the tangent plane. Standalone measures **0.0°**.

items.title: Day and night

items.body:
The rain map is a **climatology** — how much falls here in a year, averaged. Right for where
forests grow, wrong for whether you are getting wet, exactly as the temperature map was an
annual mean and needed a day laid over it.

**Rare and violent, not steady**, and two sources already in the library say so about *Earth's
deserts* as much as about Titan. Lunine and Lorenz (2009): rainfall in deserts "is expressed in
rare but violent storms". Charnay et al. (2015): "such rare and strong events may play or have
played an important role in some dune fields on Earth." So the climatology sets how **often** it
rains, not how hard.

**One field, two thresholds.** Cloud and rain come from the same drifting noise, cloud at the
lower threshold — so cloud arrives before the rain, outstays it, and appears on days it never
rains, and it can never rain from a clear sky. Deriving them separately is the same class of
mistake as a clock that disagreed with the sun.

**It closes the chain the day/night work started from.** Convection is driven by surface
heating, so storms build through the afternoon and die overnight. One multiplier, which is the
honest amount of that chain this carries.

**Cloud flattens the day both ways** — shading at noon, blanketing at midnight — applied to the
swing and not the mean, because cloud does not change how warm a place is, only how far it
moves. It is why a desert under a clear sky swings enormously and a cloudy night does not frost.
It also dims the sun, which is the visible half.

Rain costs heat (wet clothing conducts it away; a roof cancels it rather than diluting it) and
can be drunk, clean — distilled on the way up rather than filtered on the way down.

No simulation and no state: noise over position and time, drifting. Two places agree about the
sky without talking, and a save stores nothing.

**A bug the tests caught, worth keeping.** The first version assumed the terrain noise was
uniform on [-1, 1] and set the storm threshold at 0.82 of it. Measured, the field runs -0.56 to
+0.51 with σ ≈ 0.19 — Gaussian, nothing like uniform — so the threshold sat past its maximum and
**it never rained anywhere on the planet**. The intensity function now pushes the noise through
a normal CDF first, so `MaxWetFraction` means literally what it says.
`Basin.Climate.WeatherNoiseShape` reports the distribution and fails if the terrain noise ever
changes under it. The drift constant was also 11,000 m/s — 11 km/s — which moved the sample so
far through the field it stopped varying; it is 400.
items.done_when: 51 automation tests. It never rains from a clear sky (0 of 4,000 samples), the wettest ground is dry 65%+ of the time, afternoons storm more than nights, and rain both costs heat and can be drunk.

First of three items under ADR-0024 (crafting is data the desk edits). The roadmap's Phase 3 order is needs -> mining -> **crafting** -> shelter; shelter (3.14), farming (3.12) and cooking (3.13) are built and this was never a row. `UBasinInventory::Take` returns what it actually took, which is what a recipe consumes.

Scope of THIS item: the data file, the import commandlet, the consuming C++ and its tests. No simulator (3.22), no desk view (3.23). Plan mode: it adds a class under Source/. Recipe *names* are design; the *inputs* are geology and must already exist as `EBasinResource` values or biomass forage.

**Done 2026-09-06.** Recipes are data (ADR-0024): `docs/design/recipes.json` is the one home, `Tools/ue/import_recipes.py`
fills `/Game/Basin/Data/DA_Recipes`, and `UBasinCrafter` (component beside the inventory, Config asset path in
DefaultGame.ini) reads only the asset. Three recipes with an effect the code had a hole for: **cord** (2 forage),
**pick** (2 granite + cord; `FBasinMining::PickYield` doubles a swing), **charcoal** (2 forage at a fire;
`FBasinFire::FuelPerCharcoal` = 3 forage's worth of burning, so a night's warmth stops costing a harvest).

Evidence: editor build passes; `Automation RunTests Basin.Craft+Basin.Survival` 33/33 (6 Craft); `verify_planet`
**42 checks** incl. `recipes match the file: 3 recipes, identical`; `system_map.py --check` 0 problems and **2** when a
recipe was edited to `unobtainium` / a rock output, then reverted; `-BasinCraftShot` log:
`mine: granite +1` x3 -> `craft: cord` -> `craft: pick` -> `build: lit a fire` -> `craft: cord (at the fire)` ->
`craft: charcoal (at the fire)` -> `mine: sediment +2 ... with a pick`; HUD `carrying sediment 2 granite 1 forage 12
cord 1 pick 1 charcoal 1` (media, phase 3).

Two things the probe taught: the one-key rule "first affordable in asset order" could never reach charcoal while
forage lasted, so it is now "what the pack has none of, then the first affordable" (pinned by
`Basin.Craft.OneKeyFillsTheGapsFirst`); and a `UActorComponent` reads `Config` from DefaultEngine.ini unless the class
says `Config=Game`, which cost one verify run. Not done here: a touch button for craft (the same gap jump had until
2.11); a HUD line naming what is craftable (the HUD file belonged to a parallel session's uncommitted work, so the
pack line carries the evidence); the fourth recipe (fired brick), left for 3.22's simulator to judge.

items.body:
Second of three under ADR-0024. The C++ already has pure functions for the drains (FBasinDrain), mining yield (what the rock map says), farm yield (biomass) and cooking (a multiplier); the simulator re-states them in Python so a designer can ask 'what does this recipe cost here and what does it buy' without the engine. The cross-check is the same pattern as Basin.CubeSphere.MatchesBaker: one fixture, two implementations, one number. Depends on 3.19 for the recipe file.

**Done 2026-09-06.** `Tools/design/sim.py` re-states the C++ pure functions -- every constant names its C++ home, and a
test refuses one that does not. A place comes from the bake the way the engine reads it: nearest texel of `SPacked`
(rock, temperature, flux) and `GPacked` (water depth, NPP) on `export.py`'s face grid, decoded with `meta.json`'s
ranges; pO2 is the card's, as in `SampleEnvironment`. `place_from_site` reads `site.json` (the spawn), `best_farmland`
takes the max-NPP texel across the six faces, `place_from_bake(lat, lon)` anything else.

`project(recipe, place)` gives gather seconds (swings at `SwingSeconds`, gatherings at the same cadence -- the one
stated assumption; crafted inputs recursively; `FuelToLight` forage for a fire recipe), the hunger the forage would have
bought eaten raw, a value by output (charcoal: net fire seconds over burning the forage, warmth-minutes bought at this
place; pick: rock/min bare vs with, swings to repay; cord: what it enables) and flags `unreachable_here`,
`useless_here`, `ingredient`, `needs_a_fire_first`.

**The cross-check.** `fixtures/sim_cases.json`: 17 constants and 10 named places (spawn-like, farmland-like, average
Home land, airless, 94 K, 502 K, unknown, beside a fire, sealed room, half insulated). `test_sim.py` requires Python to
reproduce it exactly; `Basin.Design.SimulatorAgrees` requires the C++ to agree within 1% (integers exact). Proven:
`PICK_YIELD` set to 3 -> 2 pytest failures; reverted -> 9 pass; C++ 1/1. `Tools/check.py`'s first layer now runs
`pytest Tools/baker Tools/design`; the desk's baker command too.

**What the report said about Home** (`sim.py report`): the spawn is granite at 273.1 K annual mean with nothing growing,
so cord, pick and charcoal are all *unreachable here* -- the granite is, the forage is not. The best farmland (sediment,
295.6 K, 2,388 gDM/m2/yr) makes cord in one gathering and charcoal in two plus a fire, buys +45 s of fire over raw forage
and 1.4 min of warmth; the **pick is unreachable there because the ground is sediment**. So the pick is a *journey*:
granite from the spawn, cord from the valley. That is the first thing the simulator found that a person had not written
down, and it is what 3.23's view should put in front of a designer. Also learned: the bake's temperature is the annual
mean; the game adds half the diurnal range (ADR-0023), which is why the HUD has read 264 K at night where the report
says 273.

Not done here: the desk view (3.23); bilinear sampling (nearest texel is one 18.6 km texel of difference, stated);
a `free` flag (dropped -- gather seconds already says it).

items.body:
Third of three under ADR-0024, and the one the user asked for: a recipe 'directly actionable from the UI'. Thin by design: the backend is 3.19 (data + import) and 3.22 (simulator); this adds the view, a file watcher, and the push button that chains the existing runner. Live update of a *running* editor is deferred (Remote Control API) and recorded in the ADR's revisit trigger. Depends on 3.19 and 3.22.

**Done 2026-09-06.** The view is `Tools/desk/src/design.ts`: recipe list and editor on the
left (inputs as resource+count rows, output, count, station, note; Apply to draft), projection on the right from
`sim.py report --json` (places with drains, every recipe's gather seconds, hunger forgone, value and flags, the
breakdown under the selected recipe), a lat/lon box to sample more places. **Save** writes `docs/design/recipes.json`
through Rust and returns `system_map.py --check`'s recipe lines in words. **Push to game** runs the new `recipes` QA
suite: `import-recipes` (new catalogue command) -> `Basin.Craft` -> `verify-planet`, so the asset==file check closes
the loop. A 4-second poll of a tree stamp (docs/tracker, docs/design, docs/media, Saved/Screenshots) reloads the window
when any other writer touches the files; the poll pauses while a form is open.

Evidence: `sim.py report --json --place 45,10` returns 3 recipes x 3 places; pytest 9/9; tsc clean; cargo test 8/8;
the release exe builds; **seen on screen** (media, phase 3): three recipes, the editor, both places with their
flags and breakdowns, the sidebar footer. An hour went into a "layout overflow" that was a cropped screenshot: the
display is 3840x2160 at 150% and a DPI-unaware capture copies only the top-left 2560x1440. The capture script is
DPI-aware now; the workarounds written on the false premise were reverted before commit. Still worth your eyes:
change a recipe's count, Apply, watch the right-hand numbers move; then Save and Push. Live update of a *running* editor stays deferred
(ADR-0024 revisit trigger); Push re-imports through the commandlet.

items.body:
Asked for 2026-09-06: the desk 'needs to act as a library of resources used in all other games -- the tens of PDFs each documenting the science -- and an indexation system for easy explanations and verification'. Basin already has the seed: `docs/science/sources.json` (the source of truth, 19+ credited entries), `bibliography.md` rendered from it, the PDFs (gitignored, re-fetchable by `fetch_papers.py`), a `.textcache` of extracted text, and `Tools/science/claims.py`, which indexes every claim the ledgers make and checks the checkable ones against the card and the bake. The library item is: lift that into the desk (a view and MCP tools), key it by a shared folder so a second game reads the same shelves, and make 'explain this number' one click: claim -> principle -> source page -> the check that holds it.

**Added the same afternoon:** a *research action*. From the desk or over MCP, "research this theme" runs the same
selection process the Basin library was built with (`docs/science/`: fetch, open, credit from the PDF's own title
page, record in `sources.json`, extract to the text cache), and adds what that process did by hand: recency, the
authors' credentials checked against what can be verified (affiliation, prior work in the field, the venue),
and a contradictions pass against the papers already on the shelf -- the `contradictions.md` discipline as a
step rather than a chore. The output is a candidate list a person accepts into the library, never an automatic
addition: the library is what the game's numbers rest on, and a paper gets onto it by being read.
items.done_when: desk.json names a library (sources.json, the PDFs folder, the text cache, the claims index); the desk has a Library view listing every source with title, credit, topics, which claims cite it and which items/ADRs read it, opening the PDF or its text; a claim can be traced to its source and to the check that verifies it (claims.py's section/card/delivered); desk_library_search over MCP returns sources and claims by keyword; a second project can point its desk.json at the same library folder and see the same shelves. And a research action: given a theme, propose recent, credentialed sources by the same selection process, with a contradictions pass against the shelf, as candidates a person accepts.

claims.principle: the same calculation. A despin time only ~2.6× the
claims.text: **The day is long — 32 h, not 24** ← the same calculation. A despin time only ~2.6× the system's age means Home is *partially* despun: measurably slowed, not stopped. Earth's own day is lengthening ~1.7 ms/century under lunar tides; Home has had longer, closer, and a large moon.

claims.claim: A big moon holds the 19° tilt steady
claims.principle: a massive satellite stabilises obliquity against
claims.text: **A big moon holds the 19° tilt steady** ← a massive satellite stabilises obliquity against chaotic diffusion driven by planetary perturbations; without one, obliquity wanders. This is the standard Earth–Moon result. [Laskar, Joutel & Robutel, *Nature* 1993 — stabilisation of Earth's obliquity by the Moon]. Stable tilt is why Home gets ordered 30-day seasons instead of climate chaos, which is what makes the temperature map worth baking at all.

claims.text: **Free O₂ at 22% means a biosphere, not geology** ← molecular oxygen is not stable in quantity without continuous replenishment; it oxidises rock and reacts away. A sustained 22% atmosphere therefore *asserts* a productive photosynthetic biosphere. This is the standard O₂-as-biosignature argument, and it is a constraint on the fiction as much as a gift: Home must have a deep, old, planet-wide flora before the player arrives.

claims.text: **Photosynthesis works fine under an orange dwarf** ← directly tested: garden cress and cyanobacteria show significant photosynthesis under simulated K-dwarf illumination. claims.claim: Home's flora is dark red-brown, not green and not black
claims.principle: the star peaks at 659 nm
claims.text: **Home's flora is dark red-brown, not green and not black** ← the star peaks at 659 nm (Wien, from 4400 K), so the photon flux is weighted to the red, and a pigment that absorbs broadly across the red harvests more of it than one reflecting the middle of the band. **Note the limit:** Kiang et al. modelled K2V hosts and predicted pigments peaking in the *red-orange*, with the planet looking "very similar to Earth"; only M dwarfs pushed absorbance into the near-infrared. Hearth is K5V — cooler than their K2V case, warmer than their M cases — so the darkness is an extrapolation *between* their published points, not one of their results. ADR-0012 settles this at **dark red-brown**: red-shifted past Earth green, stopping short of the black that the sources do not support. [Kiang et al., "Spectral Signatures of Photosynthesis II", *Astrobiology* 2007]

claims.claim: Noon is scalding and midnight is cryogenic
claims.principle: the gate's 270 K is a *mean* assuming heat
claims.text: **Noon is scalding and midnight is cryogenic** ← the gate's 270 K is a *mean* assuming heat is spread over the whole sphere. An airless, slowly rotating body does no such spreading: the subsolar point sits at instantaneous radiative equilibrium, which is the mean times √2, so **~382 K (109 °C) at noon**. With an 11-day night and no atmosphere to buffer, the dark side radiates down toward ~100 K, the Luna equatorial-night precedent. That ~280 K swing across one day is the survival problem this world exists to pose.

claims.claim: Life here uses silicon–oxygen backbones where carbon chains would cook
claims.principle: the Si–O bond
claims.text: **Life here uses silicon–oxygen backbones where carbon chains would cook** ← the Si–O bond (~452 kJ/mol) is stronger than C–C (~346 kJ/mol), so siloxane polymers stay intact at temperatures that break ordinary organic chains. At ~500 K that difference is the whole argument. The laboratory anchor is that biology *can* be taught this chemistry at all: Arnold's group used directed evolution on a cytochrome c from *Rhodothermus marinus* to catalyse carbon–silicon bond formation via carbene insertion into Si–H, running in vitro and in vivo and beating industrial catalysts ~15×. [Kan, Lewis, Chen & Arnold, *Science* 2016, 354(6315), 1048–1051, "Directed evolution of cytochrome c for carbon–silicon bond formation: Bringing silicon to life"]

claims.claim: Cold chemistry is slow chemistry, and that is the world's identity
claims.principle: Arrhenius: reaction
claims.text: **Cold chemistry is slow chemistry, and that is the world's identity** ← Arrhenius: reaction rate goes as exp(−Ea/RT). Dropping from Home's 282 K to 94 K, a typical 50 kJ/mol barrier slows by roughly **eighteen orders of magnitude**. The design conclusion the roadmap draws — creatures "mistaken for rocks until one turns to look" — follows directly. But note what the number really argues: a factor of 10¹⁸ is not "slow life", it is "no life". Cold biochemistry cannot simply be Home's chemistry running down; it has to use far lower activation barriers, which is a genuine constraint on how this world's biology is written, not a licence.

sources.settles: What fraction of rain becomes groundwater, and what decides it. Precipitation and potential evapotranspiration carry the prediction; the numbers are the calibration a baker stage can be checked against.

carries Haitjema and Mitchell-Bruker's (2005) criterion, cited here SECOND-HAND because that paper is paywalled: high permeability with low recharge gives a water table controlled by recharge rather than terrain; low permeability with high recharge gives one that follows the surface

recipes.name: Cord
recipes.note: Twisted plant fibre. The first thing anyone makes, and the thing every tool is bound with. Costs forage, which is also food, seed, compost and fuel -- so the first cord is a meal not eaten.

recipes.name: Stone pick
recipes.note: A granite head bound to a handle. Carrying one doubles what a swing takes out of the ground (FBasinMining::PickYield). Granite because the spawn stands on it and because continental basement is the hard rock; a softer stone would not hold an edge.

recipes.name: Charcoal
recipes.note: Forage charred beside a lit fire. One unit burns for three forage's worth (FBasinFire::FuelPerCharcoal), so a night's warmth stops costing tomorrow's harvest -- which is the tension the fire was built to create, and this is the first way to ease it.
